content: 1. For severe hypertension, administer an appropriate antihypertensive medication immediately and refer the patient urgently to a hospital for further management. 2. For moderate hypertension, reassess the patient in one week. If hypertension persists, refer the patient to a hospital. 3. If blood pressure is normal, no additional treatment is required. 4. In postpartum care, respond to observed signs or volunteered problems. If diastolic blood pressure is elevated, check for anemia if pallor is present. 5. Review the patient’s medical records for any history of bleeding during pregnancy, delivery, or postpartum. Ask if the patient has experienced heavy bleeding since delivery or if they tire easily. 6. Measure hemoglobin levels if there is a history of bleeding. Examine for conjunctival and palmar pallor. If pallor is present, assess its severity (severe or mild). 7. For severe anemia, prescribe a double dose of iron (60 mg twice daily) for three months, refer the patient urgently to a hospital, and follow up in two weeks to monitor clinical progress and treatment compliance. 8. For moderate anemia, prescribe a double dose of iron for three months and reassess at the next postnatal visit (in four weeks). If anemia persists, refer the patient to a hospital. 9. If hemoglobin levels are above 11 g/dL and there is no anemia, continue iron treatment for a total of three months. 10. For postpartum care, check the patient’s HIV status. If the patient has not been tested, does not know their status, or tested negative early in pregnancy, offer HIV testing and counseling. 11. If the patient has taken antiretroviral (ARV) drugs during pregnancy or childbirth, refer both the patient and their baby to HIV services for further assessment. 12. Provide key information about HIV, including its transmission, the benefits of knowing one’s status, and the confidentiality of test results. Inform the patient that HIV testing is routine, like other blood tests. 13. If the patient tests positive for HIV, counsel them on the implications of the result, refer them to HIV services for further assessment and treatment initiation, and provide additional care, including counseling on infant feeding, family planning, safer sex practices, and partner testing. Follow up in two weeks. 14. If the patient tests negative for HIV, counsel them on the importance of staying negative through safer sex practices, including condom use, and encourage partner testing. 15. If the patient refuses testing or does not disclose previous test results, counsel them on safer sex practices and the benefits of partner testing. 16. For postpartum bleeding lasting more than six weeks, refer the patient to a hospital. 17. If the patient has fever or foul-smelling lochia, assess for uterine infection by checking for heavy bleeding, foul-smelling discharge, abdominal tenderness, abnormal lochia, elevated temperature, or stiff neck. Insert an IV line, administer fluids rapidly, give appropriate IM/IV antibiotics, and refer urgently to a hospital. 18. For upper urinary tract infections, administer appropriate IM/IV antibiotics and refer urgently to a hospital. 19. For lower urinary tract infections, prescribe appropriate oral antibiotics, encourage increased fluid intake, and follow up in two days. If there is no improvement, refer the patient to a hospital. 20. For very severe febrile disease, insert an IV line, administer appropriate IM/IV antibiotics, give artemether IM (or quinine IM if artemether is unavailable) and glucose, and refer urgently to a hospital. 21. For malaria, administer oral antimalarial medication and follow up in two days. If there is no improvement, refer the patient to a hospital. 22. For postpartum depression (usually after two weeks), provide emotional support and refer the patient urgently to a hospital. 23. For postpartum blues (usually within the first week), reassure the patient that this is common, listen to their concerns, provide emotional encouragement, and counsel the partner and family to assist the patient. Follow up in two weeks and refer if there is no improvement. 24. For vaginal discharge four weeks after delivery, assess for itching at the vulva, partner urinary problems, and abnormal vaginal discharge (amount, color, odor). If gonorrhea or chlamydia infection is suspected, treat both the patient and their partner with appropriate oral antibiotics and counsel on safer sex practices. 25. If a candida infection is suspected, prescribe clotrimazole and counsel on safer sex practices. If there is no improvement, refer the patient to a hospital. 26. If bacterial or trichomonas infection is suspected, prescribe metronidazole and counsel on safer sex practices. 27. For cough or breathing difficulty, assess the duration of symptoms, presence of chest pain, blood in sputum, breathlessness, or wheezing. If pneumonia is suspected, administer the first dose of appropriate IM/IV antibiotics and refer urgently to a hospital. 28. If chronic lung disease is suspected, refer the patient to a hospital for assessment. Counsel on smoking cessation if applicable. 29. For tuberculosis, reassure the patient that anti-tuberculosis drugs are safe for the baby and emphasize the importance of continuing treatment. If the patient’s sputum is TB-positive within two months of delivery, plan to give INH prophylaxis to the newborn. Offer HIV testing if not already done. Counsel on smoking cessation and screen close contacts for tuberculosis. 30. For preventive measures, ensure tetanus toxoid immunization is up to date. If the patient’s immunization status is unknown, administer TT1 and plan for TT2 in four weeks. Explain the safety of the vaccine during pregnancy and its benefits. 31. Provide iron and folic acid supplementation to all pregnant, postpartum, and post-abortion women. Dispense a three-month supply and advise on safe storage. Address any misconceptions about iron treatment and provide guidance on managing side effects. 32. For women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, administer aspirin (75 mg daily) and calcium (1500 mg daily) from 12 weeks of pregnancy until delivery. Dispense a three-month supply at each visit. 33. Administer mebendazole (500 mg) once every six months to all women, except during the first trimester. 34. Motivate adherence to treatments by addressing misconceptions and exploring the patient’s concerns. Provide clear instructions on medication use and side effect management. If necessary, involve family members or community health workers to support the patient.
